chunks: Asymmetrical half-bridge vs symmetrical H-bridge. The question: When can you use an asymmetrical half-bridge? When do you need a symmetrical H-bridge?
A half-bridge is one pair of switches that connects its output to the supply or to ground.
"Asymmetrical" here means the two halves do unequal jobs: either the two switches are sized differently, or the load only ever sees one polarity.
A symmetrical H-bridge has four equal switches and drives a load in both directions.
Imagine two workers sharing a shift. One works 90% of the day and the other 10%. You would give the busy one the better tools, not split the budget evenly.

A buck converter (a circuit that steps a voltage down by switching) is like that at low duty cycle: the low-side switch carries current most of the time, so it deserves a bigger, lower-resistance switch.
But if both workers must do the same job in turn, as in a reversing motor or a transformer, you want identical workers.
The gain from asymmetry grows as the duty cycle moves away from 50% and is symmetric about it (a low-side-dominated converter and a high-side-dominated one both gain).
At 50% duty there is nothing to gain.
Duty cycle ( D ): the fraction of each cycle the high-side switch is on. On-resistance ( R DS(on) ): the small resistance of a switch that is on; current through it makes heat.
Conduction loss: heat from current in that resistance, P equals I squared R times the fraction of time it conducts.
Unipolar vs bipolar: the load sees one voltage polarity, or both. Volt-seconds: voltage multiplied by time; a transformer needs these to average to zero.
Take a buck converter with D equals 0. 1 and a 10 amps load. Two equal 10 milliohms switches give 10 squared times (0. 1 times 0. 01 plus 0. 9 times 0. 01) equals 1. 0 watts.
Now keep the same total switch size but make the high side 20 milliohms and the low side 6. 67 milliohms. The loss becomes 100 times (0. 1 times 0. 02 plus 0. 9 times 0.
00667) equals 0. 8 watts, a 20% saving. At D equals 0. 5 equal switches are already the best. That is the whole idea.

"An asymmetrical half-bridge is one where the two FETs differ or where the load only sees one polarity, so I'd use it for unidirectional loads and buck converters at lopsided duty cycles; resizing the FETs to match the duty cycle cuts conduction loss, 20% at D = 0.

I need a symmetrical H-bridge when the load must see both polarities or zero DC average: reversing motors, voice coils, class-D speakers and transformers, where equal FETs and symmetrical drive are the right choice."
